name: Primitives

hero.title: One Toggle. The real iOS switch and the real Android switch.
hero.lede: One name per idea: Stack, Text, Field, Toggle, Modal and the rest. On the web they render plain DOM; in a native build the compiler emits the platform's own SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose views from the same .tsx.

why.title: Learn one vocabulary. Ship three kinds of UI.

items.title: One name per idea
items.text: `<Stack>`, not View, VStack, Column or div. `onPress` on every target, not onClick here and action there. `value` plus `onChangeText` for every text field.

items.title: Native, not imitated
items.text: `<Toggle>` becomes SwiftUI `Toggle` and Compose `Switch`. `<Modal>` becomes a `.sheet` and a `Dialog`. `<Field kind="password">` becomes `SecureField`. When the OS restyles its controls, your app follows.

items.title: Accessibility that reaches the device
items.text: `accessibilityLabel` becomes `aria-label`, SwiftUI `.accessibilityLabel` and a Compose `contentDescription`. `data-testid` becomes an accessibility identifier and a `testTag`, so one id drives Playwright, XCUITest and Compose tests.

items.title: Escape hatches included
items.text: `<Web>`, `<NativeIOS>` and `<NativeAndroid>` render a branch on one target only. `useNativeModule` calls your own Swift or Kotlin. `<WebView>` hosts a web-only component, with `data` in and `onMessage` out.

difference.title: One screen. Today you write it three times.

before.label: web/Signup.tsx · ios/Signup.swift · android/Signup.kt
before.caption: The same sign-up form in React, SwiftUI and Compose. Three files, three state models, three reviews for every change.

after.label: src/Signup.tsx
after.caption: One file. The Swift and Kotlin the compiler emits for it have the same shape as the hand-written two on the left: VStack(spacing: 12), Column with spacedBy(12.dp), a TextField with the email keyboard.

extraSectionsHtml:
pairs with

Design System

Primitives keep a small, fixed token scale so every target agrees on the numbers. When you want your own look, wrap them: styled(Stack) and rocketstyle chains over a primitive lower to SwiftUI and Compose as well. Web-only apps that need breakpoints and theme-aware CSS use the Design System's elements directly.

Explore the Design System →How one codebase ships three apps

demo.title: Pick a primitive, see all three outputs.
demo.text: What each primitive becomes on each platform, taken from the compiler's own output (abridged: the real emit adds tokens, accessibility and modifiers).
demo.spec: Same picker as the reference, with mappings checked against the native compiler on main: Field on iOS is `TextField("", text: Binding(…))`; Toggle on the web is `<input type="checkbox" role="switch">`; Modal on the web is a `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` (not the `open` attribute, which is non-modal); Tabs emit the `PyreonTabs` runtime, a `TabView` on iOS and Material `BottomNavigation` below 600dp / `NavigationRail` from 600dp on Android. Gesture, Select and Tabs carry a small "next release" tag. Label the panel "illustrative, abridged".

items.name: Layout:
items.text: Stack, Inline, Layer, Scroll and Spacer become VStack, HStack, ZStack and ScrollView on iOS, Column, Row and Box on Android

items.name: Content:
items.text: Text, Heading, Image, Icon, Audio and Video; `Image` loads remote URLs with AsyncImage on both platforms

items.name: Press:
items.text: tap, long press and left or right swipes on any element, through each platform's own gesture recognisers on iOS and Android and with Enter and Space on the web

items.name: Field:
items.text: text, email, number, tel, url, search and password keyboards, plus `multiline` for a text area

items.name: Dates and times:
items.text: `<Field kind="date" | "time" | "datetime">` with `min` and `max`: DatePicker on iOS, Material 3 pickers on Android, a wall-clock string everywhere

items.name: Select:
items.text: one choice from a list: `<select>`, a menu Picker, a Material 3 exposed dropdown

items.name: Tabs and Split:
items.text: tabs stay mounted when you switch away, and `createRouter({ tabs })` gives every tab its own back stack

items.name: Gesture and Canvas:
items.text: pan, pinch and rotate feeding `translateX`, `scale` and `rotate`; vector shapes with full SVG path data

items.name: Transition and TransitionGroup:
items.text: seven named presets, animated with CSS on the web, `.transition` on iOS and `AnimatedVisibility` on Android

items.name: WebView:
items.text: host a chart or editor in the native app, with `data` pushed in without a reload and `onMessage` back out

limits.title: The compiler reads your source, not npm
limits.text: Native builds lower your components in a declarative subset of TypeScript. Code outside it almost always gets a named warning; DOM-bound libraries stay on the web or go in a `<WebView>`.

limits.title: A fixed token scale
limits.text: Spacing, colour and radius come from one built-in scale with no responsive props. For breakpoints and theme-aware CSS on the web, use the Design System's elements directly.

limits.title: Some props are web-only
limits.text: `justify` and `wrap` on a Stack have no SwiftUI equivalent, so iOS and Android ignore them and the compiler says so. Put a `<Spacer />` between children to push them apart.

limits.title: Native is experimental
limits.text: The multiplatform guide keeps a gated matrix of what is device-proven. Check it before you plan a release around a primitive.

comingFrom.title: The names feel familiar. What ships is different.
comingFrom.note: `onPress` and `onChangeText` carry over. React Native runs your JavaScript on the device; here the compiler emits SwiftUI and Compose source and the import is only a type anchor. The trade: only a declarative subset of TypeScript compiles, and compiled code cannot be updated over the air. The same file also renders as a web page.

recipes.title: A booking form with each platform's own pickers
recipes.text: A date field bounded to one calendar year and a room picker with one option disabled. iOS gets a DatePicker and a menu Picker, Android gets Material 3 dialogs and an exposed dropdown, the web gets `<input type="date">` and `<select>`. The value is the same `YYYY-MM-DD` string on all three.

recipes.title: A settings screen with a native confirm sheet
recipes.text: A labelled switch pushed to the trailing edge, and a destructive action behind a confirmation. On the web the dialog is a modal `<dialog>` with focus trapping; on iOS it is a sheet you can swipe away; on Android a `Dialog`.
recipes.code:
import { signal } from '@pyreon/reactivity'
import { Stack, Inline, Toggle, Text, Button, Modal, Spacer } from '@pyreon/primitives'

export function Settings() {
  const notify = signal(true)
  const confirm = signal(false)
  return (
    <Stack gap="md" padding={4}>
      <Inline gap="sm" align="center">
        <Text>Notifications</Text>
        <Spacer />
        <Toggle value={notify()} onChange={(v) => notify.set(v)} accessibilityLabel="Notifications" />
      </Inline>
      <Button variant="danger" onPress={() => confirm.set(true)}>Delete account</Button>
      <Modal open={confirm()} onClose={() => confirm.set(false)}>
        <Stack gap="md" padding={4}>
          <Text>Delete your account? This cannot be undone.</Text>
          <Button variant="ghost" onPress={() => confirm.set(false)}>Cancel</Button>
        </Stack>
      </Modal>
    </Stack>
  )
}

faq.a: No. React Native runs your JavaScript on the device. Here the compiler reads your `.tsx` at build time and writes SwiftUI and Compose source; on native targets the `@pyreon/primitives` import is only there for TypeScript. On the web, the same file renders plain DOM.

faq.q: Can I use my own theme?
faq.a: The primitives' own props use a fixed scale (`gap="md"` is 12 everywhere) so every target agrees. For your own look, `styled(Stack)` and rocketstyle chains over a primitive also lower to native. Web-only apps with breakpoints and theme-aware CSS should use the Design System's elements instead.

faq.q: What happens to code that cannot compile to native?
faq.a: The compiler almost always names it in a warning, for example `justify` or `wrap` on a Stack. Code that needs the DOM goes behind `<Web>` or inside a `<WebView>`.

faq.q: Can I drop down to Swift or Kotlin?
faq.a: Yes, through `defineNativeModule` and `useNativeModule`, which call a Swift or Kotlin class you own. `<NativeIOS>` and `<NativeAndroid>` only choose which primitives render per platform; they do not take raw Swift.

faq.q: Is it ready for my production app?
faq.a: The web side is pre-1.0, with the same stability rules as the rest of the framework. The native targets are experimental, and the multiplatform guide says so in its status line. The device-test matrix there is the source of truth for what is proven.
